notes: The with_skill win is driven almost entirely by one behavior: actually running the result in a headless browser. In all 3 cases, the with-skill run installed Playwright and verified at 375/768/1440px; in all 3 baseline runs, the agent either skipped verification entirely or only opened the file without checking console errors, interactions, or viewport widths.

In every with-skill run, real bugs were caught and fixed only because of that browser verification: oversized checkmark icons (pricing page), an SVG 'hidden' attribute/property quirk that stacked both eye-icon states (login form), and a mobile horizontal-overflow bug from a flex auto-margin interacting with an unwrapped table (dashboard). None of these would have been visible from a code read-back alone, which is exactly the failure mode the baseline runs fell into.

The cost is real: with_skill runs took roughly 6-9x longer (512-731s vs 57-160s) and used ~1.7x the tokens (~91-104k vs ~52-64k), almost entirely from installing Playwright/Chromium fresh in each sandbox and iterating on a found bug. In a repo that already has browser tooling available this gap should shrink a lot, since most of the time cost here is one-time environment setup rather than inherent to the verification step.

Completeness (requested elements, inferred features like validation states) was fairly close between with- and without-skill on these particular prompts, 2/3 baseline runs implemented validation/loading states unprompted. The skill's distinguishing value here is specifically the 'no bugs / responsive confirmed' half of its promise, not raw feature coverage, at least for prompts of this complexity.

The dashboard-in-existing-site case is the cleanest signal: both runs matched the existing plain-HTML/CSS stack and built equivalent content, so the only real differentiator was verification; without_skill explicitly shipped an unfixed mobile table overflow bug as a 'caveat' rather than catching it.
